new_statements.translation: TONES. For the moment, in this domain, we will limit ourselves to pointing out that we have noted three distinct levels: high, mid and low, and that they do not seem to combine with a stress (intensity) accent. But we will need to complete our survey before we can say whether the three levels noted are phonological or phonetic, given the modifications that occur and that are tied to morpho-syntactic rules. There are also, on long vowels, melodic (contour) realisations, generally of rising register.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The subsection LES TONS reads exactly as quoted: 'Pour le moment, dans ce domaine, nous nous contenterons de souligner que nous avons note trois niveaux distincts : haut, moyen et bas, et qu'ils ne semblent pas se combiner avec un accent d'intensite. Mais il nous sera necessaire de completer notre enquete avant de pouvoir dire si les trois niveaux notes sont phonologiques ou phonetiques, compte-tenu des modifications qui interviennent et qui sont liees a des regles morpho-syntaxiques. Il existe aussi, sur les voyelles longues, des realisations melodiques de registre generalement montant.' The only quirk is that 'des' before 'regles' is a handwritten insertion above the line in the scan; the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shanga (like Tyanga/Kyenga) is a three-level register tone language (H, M, L, plus rising contours on long vowels); the author found no stress accent operating alongside the tones, i.e. no word-level intensity prominence. No position for stress is given because none was observed. The claim is hedged ('ne semblent pas') and the tone analysis itself is declared provisional.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author notes tone modifications tied to morpho-syntactic rules and that base tones of most lexemes could not yet be determined.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/lexeme level, based on c. 1,000 words per lect elicited partly in isolation and mostly in short phrases at Sakaci (shanga) and Kasaci (tyanga), Nigeria; one phonetic inventory presented as valid for both lects. Jones 2010 (independent, p. 11 and p. 19) confirms three level lexical tones with every syllable tone-bearing and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Platiel 1982 describes two lects together: tyanga (= Kyenga/Kyanga, glottocode kyen1242, ISO tye, village Kasaci) and shanga (= Shanga, shan1282, ISO sho, village Sakaci, Nigeria). The phonetic inventory and the LES TONS statement are explicitly presented as one table/analysis 'valable pour les deux parlers', so the statement applies to Shanga but is not Shanga-specific; Jones 2010 treats Shanga phonology as 'similar to Kyanga' with three level tones.

sources.note: Sec. 2 (pp. 85-91, one phonetic inventory stated valid for both tyanga and shanga, data c. 1,000 words per lect from Kasaci and Sakaci), subsection LES TONS p. 91: three distinct tone levels (high, mid, low) noted, 'et qu'ils ne semblent pas se combiner avec un accent d'intensite' (they do not seem to combine with a stress accent); analysis explicitly provisional; rising melodic realisations on long vowels. Tone marks are omitted from the wordlists because base tones could not yet be determined.

sources.note: Kyanga sec. 7.0 Phonology pp. 10-12, 'Tone' p. 11: three level lexical tones H/M/L, every syllable has a tone, polysyllabic nouns tend to be all mid, many words have lost tone vs Boko/Busa; acute/grave in the orthography mark tone. Shanga sec. 5.0 Phonology p. 19: 'The phonology is similar to Kyanga, except for the following' (four segmental points). Nothing on stress or accent for either lect.
